claim: Platelets use receptor glycoprotein Ib (GPIb), specifically its α subunit (GPIbα), to signal as they tether and translocate on von Willebrand factor (VWF) of injured arterial surfaces against blood flow.
source: Platelets use receptor glycoprotein Ib (GPIb), specifically its α subunit (GPIbα), to signal as they tether and translocate on von Willebrand factor (VWF) of injured arterial surfaces against blood flow.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the biological function of GPIbα, supported by the experimental design and results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Force elicits catch bonds to slow VWF–GPIbα dissociation.
source: Force elicits catch bonds to slow VWF–GPIbα dissociation and unfolds the GPIbα leucine-rich repeat domain (LRRD) and juxtamembrane mechanosensitive domain (MSD).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing force-dependent bond lifetimes and references to prior work.

claim: Force unfolds the GPIbα leucine-rich repeat domain (LRRD).
source: Force elicits catch bonds to slow VWF–GPIbα dissociation and unfolds the GPIbα leucine-rich repeat domain (LRRD) and juxtamembrane mechanosensitive domain (MSD).
evidence: This is supported by direct experimental measurements of LRRD unfolding shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Force unfolds the GPIbα juxtamembrane mechanosensitive domain (MSD).
source: Force elicits catch bonds to slow VWF–GPIbα dissociation and unfolds the GPIbα leucine-rich repeat domain (LRRD) and juxtamembrane mechanosensitive domain (MSD).
evidence: This is supported by direct experimental measurements of MSD unfolding shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: LRRD unfolding intensifies Ca2+ signal.
source: Here we analyze these extracellular events and the resulting intracellular Ca2+ on a single platelet in real time, revealing that LRRD unfolding intensifies Ca2+ signal whereas MSD unfolding affects the type of Ca2+ signal.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing correlation between LRRD unfolding and Ca2+ signal intensity.

claim: MSD unfolding affects the type of Ca2+ signal.
source: Here we analyze these extracellular events and the resulting intracellular Ca2+ on a single platelet in real time, revealing that LRRD unfolding intensifies Ca2+ signal whereas MSD unfolding affects the type of Ca2+ signal.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5-7 showing that MSD unfolding determines whether α-type or β-type Ca2+ signals are triggered.

claim: LRRD is an analog force transducer.
source: Therefore, LRRD and MSD are analog and digital force transducers, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that LRRD unfolding leads to continuous alterations in signal level.

claim: MSD is a digital force transducer.
source: Therefore, LRRD and MSD are analog and digital force transducers, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that MSD unfolding results in binary decision of Ca2+ type (α vs β).

claim: The macroglycopeptide separating LRRD and MSD is >30 nm in length.
source: The >30 nm macroglycopeptide separating the two domains transmits force on the VWF–GPIbα bond (whose lifetime is prolonged by LRRD unfolding) to the MSD to enhance its unfolding, resulting in unfolding cooperativity at an optimal force.
evidence: This is based on the known structure of GPIbα and is consistent with the observed unfolding lengths.

claim: The macroglycopeptide transmits force from the VWF–GPIbα bond to the MSD.
source: The >30 nm macroglycopeptide separating the two domains transmits force on the VWF–GPIbα bond (whose lifetime is prolonged by LRRD unfolding) to the MSD to enhance its unfolding, resulting in unfolding cooperativity at an optimal force.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation of cooperative unfolding between spatially separated domains.

claim: LRRD unfolding prolongs VWF–GPIbα bond lifetime.
source: The >30 nm macroglycopeptide separating the two domains transmits force on the VWF–GPIbα bond (whose lifetime is prolonged by LRRD unfolding) to the MSD to enhance its unfolding, resulting in unfolding cooperativity at an optimal force.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B showing longer bond lifetimes when LRRD unfolds.

claim: LRRD unfolding enhances MSD unfolding.
source: The >30 nm macroglycopeptide separating the two domains transmits force on the VWF–GPIbα bond (whose lifetime is prolonged by LRRD unfolding) to the MSD to enhance its unfolding, resulting in unfolding cooperativity at an optimal force.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing cooperative unfolding between LRRD and MSD.

claim: There is an optimal force for unfolding cooperativity between LRRD and MSD.
source: The >30 nm macroglycopeptide separating the two domains transmits force on the VWF–GPIbα bond (whose lifetime is prolonged by LRRD unfolding) to the MSD to enhance its unfolding, resulting in unfolding cooperativity at an optimal force.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F showing maximum cooperativity at 25 pN for A1WT.

claim: Platelets rapidly respond to changes in hydrodynamic forces and substrate stiffness due to vascular pathology.
source: Platelets can serve as a natural model system for studying cell mechanosensing as they rapidly respond to changes in hydrodynamic forces and substrate stiffness due to vascular pathology (Jackson, 2011; Qiu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GPIbα serves as a mechanoreceptor.
source: Previous studies have suggested the role of GPIbα as a mechanoreceptor, for force exerted on it via its ligand VWF induces platelet signaling (Ruggeri, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and the experimental data presented in this manuscript.

claim: Force exerted on GPIbα via VWF induces platelet signaling.
source: Previous studies have suggested the role of GPIbα as a mechanoreceptor, for force exerted on it via its ligand VWF induces platelet signaling (Ruggeri, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and experimental data in Figures 5-7.

claim: The receptor binding domain A1 is exposed by structural changes in VWF induced by elongational flow and collagen immobilization.
source: 1) Mechanopresentation: the receptor binding domain A1 is exposed by structural changes in VWF induced by elongational flow and collagen immobilization (Ju et al., 2015a; Springer, 2014);
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GPIbα LRRD receives the force signal via engaging VWF-A1 to tether the platelet against shear stress.
source: 2) Mechanoreception: GPIbα LRRD receives the force signal via engaging VWF-A1 to tether the platelet against shear stress;
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and data showing A1-GPIbα binding under force.

claim: Force is propagated from the LRRD through the mucin-like macroglycopeptide (MP) stalk and the MSD across the membrane to adaptor and signaling molecules (e.g. 14-3-3ζ) inside the platelet.
source: 3) Mechanotransmission: force is propagated from the LRRD through the mucin-like macroglycopeptide (MP) stalk (cf. Figure 2A) (Fox et al., 1988) and the MSD across the membrane to adaptor and signaling molecules (e.g. 14-3-3ζ) inside the platelet (cf. Figure 7G);
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing cooperative unfolding and the role of 14-3-3ζ in signaling.

claim: GPIbα forms catch-slip bonds with wild-type (WT) A1 in >15 pN.
source: For example, GPIbα forms catch-slip bonds with wild-type (WT) A1 in >15 pN, such that the bond lifetime first increases with force, reaches a maximum at ~25 pN, and decreases thereafter;
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and data in Figure 6G.

claim: The bond lifetime of GPIbα with wild-type A1 first increases with force, reaches a maximum at ~25 pN, and decreases thereafter.
source: For example, GPIbα forms catch-slip bonds with wild-type (WT) A1 in >15 pN, such that the bond lifetime first increases with force, reaches a maximum at ~25 pN, and decreases thereafter;
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6G showing catch-slip bond behavior.

claim: GPIbα forms slip-only bonds with type 2B von Willebrand disease (VWD) mutant A1R1450E.
source: whereas it forms slip-only bonds with type 2B von Willebrand disease (VWD) mutant (e.g. A1R1450E), such that the bond lifetime decreases monotonically with force (Ju et al., 2013; Yago et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and data in Figure 6H.

claim: The bond lifetime of GPIbα with A1R1450E decreases monotonically with force.
source: whereas it forms slip-only bonds with type 2B von Willebrand disease (VWD) mutant (e.g. A1R1450E), such that the bond lifetime decreases monotonically with force (Ju et al., 2013; Yago et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6H showing slip-only bond behavior.

claim: Force induces unfolding of the LRRD, which prolongs A1–GPIbα bond lifetime.
source: As another example, force induces unfolding of the LRRD, which prolongs A1–GPIbα bond lifetime (Ju et al., 2015b), and of the MSD, which is hypothesized to play a role in platelet signaling (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data in Figure 4B.

claim: Force induces unfolding of the MSD, which is hypothesized to play a role in platelet signaling.
source: As another example, force induces unfolding of the LRRD, which prolongs A1–GPIbα bond lifetime (Ju et al., 2015b), and of the MSD, which is hypothesized to play a role in platelet signaling (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and experimental data in Figures 5-7 showing MSD unfolding is required for α-type Ca2+ signaling.

claim: Adhesion frequencies were kept low (<20%) to ensure the platelet was pulled predominantly (>89%) by a single GPIbα bond.
source: Adhesion frequencies from these cycles were kept low (<20%) by adjusting the ligand or antibody density, a condition required for the platelet to be pulled predominantly (>89%) by a single GPIbα bond (Chesla et al., 1998; Zhu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an experimental design criterion supported by citations to prior methodology papers.

claim: Control experiments using beads lacking ligand showed no binding.
source: Control experiments using beads lacking ligand showed no binding, and blocking with mAb AK2 (epitope mapped to leucine-rich repeat 1–2 overlapping the A1 binding site, cf. Figure 2A) eliminated GPIbα binding to A1 but not to mAb WM23 (epitope mapped to the MP below LRRD, cf. Figure 2A) (Figure 1D) (Dong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: Blocking with mAb AK2 eliminated GPIbα binding to A1 but not to mAb WM23.
source: Control experiments using beads lacking ligand showed no binding, and blocking with mAb AK2 (epitope mapped to leucine-rich repeat 1–2 overlapping the A1 binding site, cf. Figure 2A) eliminated GPIbα binding to A1 but not to mAb WM23 (epitope mapped to the MP below LRRD, cf. Figure 2A) (Figure 1D) (Dong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D showing specific blocking of A1 binding.

claim: The binding site of A1 is within LRRD.
source: This confirmed binding specificity and that the binding site of A1 is within LRRD but the binding site of WM23 is outside (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the blocking experiment with AK2 and citation to prior work.

claim: The binding site of WM23 is outside LRRD.
source: This confirmed binding specificity and that the binding site of A1 is within LRRD but the binding site of WM23 is outside (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the blocking experiment showing WM23 binding was not affected by AK2.

claim: The unfolding lengths of individual ramped unfolding events distributed tri-modally with three subpopulations.
source: The lengths of individual ramped unfolding events distributed tri-modally with three subpopulations (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and statistical analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first subpopulation of ramped unfolding events corresponds to MSD unfolding.
source: The first subpopulation coincides with the ramped unfolding length distribution from WM23 vs. platelet experiments (Figure 2E, white bars).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with WM23 experiments that can only unfold MSD, and WLC model fitting in Figure 2H.

claim: WM23 binds the MP region below the LRRD.
source: WM23 binds the MP region below the LRRD (Figure 2A), hence could unfold MSD only.
evidence: This is based on known epitope mapping and is consistent with the experimental observation that WM23 only induces MSD unfolding.

claim: WM23 could unfold MSD only.
source: WM23 binds the MP region below the LRRD (Figure 2A), hence could unfold MSD only.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2E showing only one peak in the unfolding length distribution for WM23.

claim: The WLC model fit to WM23 vs. platelet data yielded a contour length of 25.99 ± 0.85 nm.
source: The average unfolding force vs. length data from the WM23 experiment was well fitted by the WLC model, yielding a contour length of 25.99 ± 0.85 nm (Figure 2H) that matches the previously reported MSD contour length (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data and model fitting shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The contour length of 25.99 ± 0.85 nm matches the previously reported MSD contour length.
source: The average unfolding force vs. length data from the WM23 experiment was well fitted by the WLC model, yielding a contour length of 25.99 ± 0.85 nm (Figure 2H) that matches the previously reported MSD contour length (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior literature.

claim: The second subpopulation of ramped unfolding events corresponds to LRRD unfolding.
source: The second subpopulation in Figure 2D matches the histogram of ramped unfolding lengths of GC pulled via A1 (Figure 2E, blue bars) that ranges from 18–56 nm and peaks at 36 nm (length of leucine-rich repeats 3–6).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with GC experiments that can only unfold LRRD, and WLC model fitting in Figure 2I.

claim: The ramped unfolding length of GC pulled via A1 ranges from 18–56 nm and peaks at 36 nm.
source: The second subpopulation in Figure 2D matches the histogram of ramped unfolding lengths of GC pulled via A1 (Figure 2E, blue bars) that ranges from 18–56 nm and peaks at 36 nm (length of leucine-rich repeats 3–6).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The WLC model fit to A1 vs. GC data yielded a best-fit contour length of 70.29 ± 3.56 nm.
source: The average unfolding force vs. length plots derived from the A1 vs. platelet and A1 vs. GC experiments overlaid well on the same WLC model fit (Figure 2I). The best-fit contour length (70.29 ± 3.56 nm) matches the length of LRRD, calculated using a 4-Å contour length per residue (Ju et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data and model fitting shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The best-fit contour length of 70.29 ± 3.56 nm matches the length of LRRD.
source: The average unfolding force vs. length plots derived from the A1 vs. platelet and A1 vs. GC experiments overlaid well on the same WLC model fit (Figure 2I). The best-fit contour length (70.29 ± 3.56 nm) matches the length of LRRD, calculated using a 4-Å contour length per residue (Ju et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with calculated LRRD length based on its structure.

claim: The third subpopulation of ramped unfolding events corresponds to concurrent unfolding of both MSD and LRRD.
source: The third subpopulation in Figure 2D can be identified as concurrent unfolding of both MSD and LRRD that occurred within too short a time elapse to be distinguished by our BFP as two separate events, because its maximum unfolding length (85 nm) matches the sum of the observed maximum MSD and LRRD unfolding lengths.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the maximum unfolding length equals the sum of MSD and LRRD lengths.

claim: The maximum unfolding length of the third subpopulation (85 nm) matches the sum of the observed maximum MSD and LRRD unfolding lengths.
source: The third subpopulation in Figure 2D can be identified as concurrent unfolding of both MSD and LRRD that occurred within too short a time elapse to be distinguished by our BFP as two separate events, because its maximum unfolding length (85 nm) matches the sum of the observed maximum MSD and LRRD unfolding lengths.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Similar tri-modally distributed ramped unfolding lengths were obtained by using mAb AN51 instead of A1 to pull the platelet GPIbα.
source: Similar tri-modally distributed ramped unfolding lengths were obtained by using mAb AN51 (epitope mapped to the N-terminal flanking region above LRRD, cf. Figure 2A) instead of A1 to pull the platelet GPIbα (Figure 2F), and the second subpopulation also matches the ramped unfolding length distribution obtained using AN51 to pull GC (Figure 2G, blue bars).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The unfolding lengths are determined by the respective primary structures of the LRRD and MSD, and as such should not depend on the 'grabbing handle' used to pull GPIbα.
source: These results are expected because the unfolding lengths are determined by the respective primary structures of the LRRD and MSD, and as such should not depend on the 'grabbing handle' used to pull GPIbα.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that A1 and AN51 produce similar unfolding length distributions.

claim: Clamped forces unfolded only MSD.
source: Interestingly, the two force waveforms induced unfolding of different GPIbα domains. Clamped forces unfolded only MSD as the lengths of clamped unfolding distribute as a single peak at 20 nm (Figure 2E,G, red bars), matching the first subpopulation in Figure 2D,F, respectively, regardless of whether platelet GPIbα was engaged by A1 or AN51.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,G.

claim: The lengths of clamped unfolding distribute as a single peak at 20 nm.
source: Interestingly, the two force waveforms induced unfolding of different GPIbα domains. Clamped forces unfolded only MSD as the lengths of clamped unfolding distribute as a single peak at 20 nm (Figure 2E,G, red bars), matching the first subpopulation in Figure 2D,F, respectively, regardless of whether platelet GPIbα was engaged by A1 or AN51.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 2E,G.

claim: Unfolding of LRRD in GC was induced only by ramped forces but not clamped forces.
source: Furthermore, unfolding of LRRD in GC was induced only by ramped forces but not clamped forces (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: Pulling platelet GPIbα via WM23 with both ramped and clamped forces induced MSD unfolding events with similar occurrence frequencies and unfolding lengths.
source: By comparison, pulling platelet GPIbα via WM23 with both ramped and clamped forces induced MSD unfolding events with similar occurrence frequencies and unfolding lengths (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: MSD can be unfolded by increasing forces as well as constant forces.
source: These results indicate that MSD can be unfolded by increasing forces as well as constant forces.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both ramped and clamped forces induce MSD unfolding.

claim: LRRD unfolding requires increasing forces.
source: By comparison, LRRD unfolding requires increasing forces.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only ramped forces, not clamped forces, induce LRRD unfolding.

claim: The ramped unfolding frequencies of both LRRD and MSD were extremely low at ≤10 pN but increased with the higher levels of clamped forces.
source: The ramped unfolding frequencies of both domains were extremely low at ≤10 pN but increased with the higher levels of clamped forces (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: LRRD unfolded more frequently when platelet GPIbα and GC were pulled by A1WT than A1R1450E.
source: Interestingly, LRRD, but not MSD, unfolded more frequently when platelet GPIbα (Figure 3A) and GC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were pulled by A1WT than A1R1450E.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ramped unfolding forces of both LRRD and MSD increased with the clamped force.
source: The ramped unfolding forces of both domains increased with the clamped force and were indifferent to whether force was applied via WT or R1450E mutant of A1 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The ramped unfolding forces of both LRRD and MSD were indifferent to whether force was applied via WT or R1450E mutant of A1.
source: The ramped unfolding forces of both domains increased with the clamped force and were indifferent to whether force was applied via WT or R1450E mutant of A1 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: A higher force was required to unfold LRRD than MSD.
source: In general, a higher force was required to unfold LRRD than MSD.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the unfolding force data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: MSD clamped unfolding frequency increases initially and decreases after reaching maximal at 25 pN when pulled by A1WT.
source: Surprisingly, pulling platelet GPIbα via different ligands generated distinctive MSD clamped unfolding frequency vs. force plots: increasing initially and decreasing after reaching maximal at 25 pN when pulled by A1WT, but decreasing monotonically when pulled by A1R1450E (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: MSD clamped unfolding frequency decreases monotonically when pulled by A1R1450E.
source: Surprisingly, pulling platelet GPIbα via different ligands generated distinctive MSD clamped unfolding frequency vs. force plots: increasing initially and decreasing after reaching maximal at 25 pN when pulled by A1WT, but decreasing monotonically when pulled by A1R1450E (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The mechanoreceptor GPIbα may be able to interpret mechanical cues and discriminate ligands by responding to different force waveforms applied via different ligands with distinct LRRD and MSD unfolding frequencies.
source: These data suggest that the mechanoreceptor GPIbα may be able to interpret mechanical cues and discriminate ligands by responding to different force waveforms applied via different ligands with distinct LRRD and MSD unfolding frequencies.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different ligands and force waveforms produce different unfolding patterns.

claim: At 25 pN, LRRD unfolding significantly enhanced MSD unfolding (p = 3.09 × 10–4).
source: At 25 pN, LRRD unfolding significantly enhanced MSD unfolding (p = 3.09 × 10–4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Significant (p = 0.05) unfolding cooperativity was observed only for A1WT at 25 and 40 pN.
source: Interestingly, significant (p = 0.05, dashed horizontal lines) unfolding cooperativity was observed only for A1WT at 25 and 40 pN.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The cooperativity between LRRD and MSD unfolding is force- and ligand-dependent.
source: These data show that the cooperativity between LRRD and MSD unfolding is force- and ligand-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cooperativity varies with force and is present for A1WT but not A1R1450E.

claim: MSD clamped, but not ramped, unfolding was significantly (p= 8.79 × 10–3 vs. 0.076 at 25 pN) enhanced by LRRD unfolding.
source: To elucidate the mechanism underlying the force- and ligand-dependent unfolding cooperativity, we note that when the MSD unfolding events were separately analyzed according to their occurrence in the ramping or clamping phase, MSD clamped, but not ramped, unfolding was significantly (p= 8.79 × 10–3 vs. 0.076 at 25 pN) enhanced by LRRD unfolding (Figure 3G), which occurred in the ramping phase only.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The dominance of cooperativity by sequential rather than concurrent unfolding suggests that LRRD unfolding impacts MSD unfolding through prolonging bond lifetime.
source: This dominance of cooperativity by sequential rather than concurrent unfolding suggests a model for LRRD unfolding to impact MSD unfolding, which includes three ideas.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MSD clamped unfolding is enhanced by prior LRRD unfolding.

claim: Force-clamp measurements revealed similar MSD time-to-unfold (tu) values induced by A1WT or A1R1450E pulling.
source: Our force-clamp measurements revealed similar tu values induced by A1WT or A1R1450E pulling (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 10 pN, a shorter tu was induced by A1WT than A1R1450E.
source: The only exception is at 10 pN where a shorter tu was induced by A1WT than A1R1450E.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The much shorter lifetime of GPIbα bond with A1WT at 10 pN may underestimate tu because early dissociation of GPIbα would prevent observation of slow MSD unfolding events.
source: This can be explained by their differential bond lifetimes (Figure 4B,C). Compared to A1R1450E, the much shorter lifetime of GPIbα bond with A1WT at 10 pN may underestimate tu because early dissociation of GPIbα would prevent observation of slow MSD unfolding events.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that bond lifetime affects the ability to observe unfolding.

claim: MSD clamped unfolding should occur before A1–GPIbα dissociation.
source: This reasoning provides the second idea for our model: MSD clamped unfolding should occur before A1–GPIbα dissociation.
evidence: This is a logical requirement for observing MSD unfolding.

claim: LRRD unfolding significantly prolongs GPIbα bond lifetime with A1WT but not A1R1450E.
source: The third idea comes from our previous observation (Ju et al., 2015b) that LRRD unfolding significantly prolongs GPIbα bond lifetime with A1WT (Figure 4B) but not A1R1450E (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The A1–GPIbα bond lifetime, regulated by force and prolonged by LRRD unfolding in respective ligand-specific manners, determines the occurrence of MSD clamped unfolding.
source: Combining these three ideas, our model proposes that the A1–GPIbα bond lifetime, regulated by force and prolonged by LRRD unfolding in respective ligand-specific manners, determines the occurrence of MSD clamped unfolding, which, despite its ligand-independent unfolding kinetics, generates a cooperativity pattern that maximizes at the optimal force of 25 pN for A1WT but not for A1R1450E.
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: The model predicts both the quantitative enhancement of MSD unfolding by LRRD unfolding for A1WT and the lack of enhancement for A1R1450E without a single freely adjustable fitting parameter.
source: Remarkably, the model predicts both the quantitative enhancement of MSD unfolding by LRRD unfolding for A1WT and the lack of enhancement for A1R1450E without a single freely adjustable fitting parameter.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The excellent agreement between theory and experiment has provided strong support for the model.
source: The excellent agreement between theory and experiment has provided strong support for our model and explained the data in Figure 4E,F.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Platelet translocation on VWF signals through GPIbα to induce Ca2+ fluxes.
source: Platelet translocation on VWF signals through GPIbα to induce Ca2+ fluxes (Mazzucato et al., 2002; Nesbitt et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Ca2+ signals were classified into three types: null-type, α-type, and β-type.
source: The Ca2+ signals over the 200-s observation window of repeated platelet contact cycles were classified into three types (Figure 5A,B): i) null-type, featured by a basal trace with a maximum Ca2+ intensity increase (normalized by its initial value) ΔImax<0.05; ii) α-type, featured by an initial latent phase followed by a spike (mostly ΔImax>0.5) with a quick decay (Video 2); iii) β-type, featured by fluctuating signals around the baseline or gradually increasing signals to an intermediate level (mostly ΔImax<0.5) followed by a gradual decay to baseline (Video 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5A,B and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: Null-type Ca2+ is featured by a basal trace with a maximum Ca2+ intensity increase ΔImax<0.05.
source: i) null-type, featured by a basal trace with a maximum Ca2+ intensity increase (normalized by its initial value) ΔImax<0.05;
evidence: This is a definition based on experimental observations.

claim: α-type Ca2+ is featured by an initial latent phase followed by a spike (mostly ΔImax>0.5) with a quick decay.
source: ii) α-type, featured by an initial latent phase followed by a spike (mostly ΔImax>0.5) with a quick decay (Video 2);
evidence: This is a definition based on experimental observations shown in Video 2.

claim: β-type Ca2+ is featured by fluctuating signals around the baseline or gradually increasing signals to an intermediate level (mostly ΔImax<0.5) followed by a gradual decay to baseline.
source: iii) β-type, featured by fluctuating signals around the baseline or gradually increasing signals to an intermediate level (mostly ΔImax<0.5) followed by a gradual decay to baseline (Video 3).
evidence: This is a definition based on experimental observations shown in Video 3.

claim: The α- and β-types match the previous characterization of platelet internal Ca2+ release triggered by VWF–GPIbα bonds measured in flow chamber experiments.
source: The null type reflects the baseline with background noise, while the α- and β-types match the previous characterization of platelet internal Ca2+release triggered by VWF–GPIbα bonds measured in flow chamber experiments (Mazzucato et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A1WT–GPIbα bonds triggered much higher ΔImax than controls when pulled by a 25 pN clamp force.
source: Pulled by a 25 pN clamp force, A1WT–GPIbα bonds triggered much higher ΔImax than controls (Figure 5C), showing 28, 42, and 30% of null-, α- and β-types, respectively (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Control experiments that merely held aspirated platelets or contacted them by beads without coating any ligand showed null-type Ca2+ only.
source: Control experiments that merely held aspirated platelets or contacted them by beads without coating any ligand showed null-type Ca2+ only (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The α-type Ca2+ could also be triggered by pulling GPIbα with AN51 but not with an anti-GPIbβ mAb.
source: The α-type Ca2+ could also be triggered by pulling GPIbα with AN51 but not with an anti-GPIbβ mAb (Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), despite that GPIbβ is tightly connected to GPIbα within one GPIb complex and has been postulated to play a role in signaling through GPIb (Strassel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: GPIbβ is tightly connected to GPIbα within one GPIb complex and has been postulated to play a role in signaling through GPIb.
source: The α-type Ca2+ could also be triggered by pulling GPIbα with AN51 but not with an anti-GPIbβ mAb (Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), despite that GPIbβ is tightly connected to GPIbα within one GPIb complex and has been postulated to play a role in signaling through GPIb (Strassel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: GPIbα engagement is necessary to trigger intraplatelet Ca2+.
source: These data demonstrated the necessity of GPIbα engagement to trigger intraplatelet Ca2+ and agree with the previous report that α-type Ca2+ peaks occur when platelets are transiently arrested in the whole blood flow (Mazzucato et al., 2002;Nesbitt et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing that only GPIbα engagement, not GPIbβ engagement, triggers Ca2+.

claim: α-type Ca2+ peaks occur when platelets are transiently arrested in the whole blood flow.
source: These data demonstrated the necessity of GPIbα engagement to trigger intraplatelet Ca2+ and agree with the previous report that α-type Ca2+ peaks occur when platelets are transiently arrested in the whole blood flow (Mazzucato et al., 2002;Nesbitt et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ΔImax correlates best with the pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetime tmax.
source: We found that ΔImax correlates best with the pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetime tmax (Figure 5E), similarly well with the pre-Ca2+ cumulative lifetime ∑ti (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), but poorly with the pre-Ca2+ average lifetime <t> (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: ΔImax correlates similarly well with the pre-Ca2+ cumulative lifetime ∑ti.
source: We found that ΔImax correlates best with the pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetime tmax (Figure 5E), similarly well with the pre-Ca2+ cumulative lifetime ∑ti (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), but poorly with the pre-Ca2+ average lifetime <t> (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ΔImax correlates poorly with the pre-Ca2+ average lifetime <t>.
source: We found that ΔImax correlates best with the pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetime tmax (Figure 5E), similarly well with the pre-Ca2+ cumulative lifetime ∑ti (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), but poorly with the pre-Ca2+ average lifetime <t> (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: For each platelet usually ∑ti could be approximated by tmax but <t> is of a smaller and variable value.
source: Careful examination of many overlaid calcium and bond lifetime traces, as exemplified in Figure 5B, revealed that the ∑ti values are generally dominated by the tmax values, which are usually much longer than the rest of the pre-Ca2+ bond lifetimes and are immediately followed by the calcium onset before observing additional shorter bond lifetimes. In other words, for each platelet usually ∑ti could be approximated by tmax but <t> is of a smaller and variable value.
evidence: This is inferred from examination of the data traces shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A single long-lived GPIbα bond is sufficient to trigger Ca2+ in a platelet.
source: Importantly, these results also suggest that a single long-lived GPIbα bond is sufficient to trigger Ca2+ in a platelet.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tmax dominates the correlation with Ca2+ and is often followed immediately by Ca2+ onset.

claim: For A1R1450E, the tmax value was significantly shorter and the α-type Ca2+ population was greatly reduced.
source: This assertion has been further supported by the parallel analysis of the data for A1R1450E. Although for R1450E the tmax value was significantly shorter and the α-type Ca2+ population was greatly reduced, the ΔImax still showed similar correlation with tmax (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetime correlates the Ca2+ strength and type.
source: Thus the pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetime correlates the Ca2+ strength and type.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis for both A1WT and A1R1450E.

claim: Only low levels of β-type Ca2+ were resulted from force-ramp experiments.
source: We first performed force-ramp experiment to generate a wide range of rupture forces using three ramping rates: 100, 1000 and 10,000 pN/s. However, only low levels of β-type Ca2+ were resulted (Figure 6A,B), showing no correlation with the largest rupture force prior to calcium onset (Figure 6C,D, right ordinate), regardless of whether platelets were tested by A1WT (Figure 6A,C) or A1R1450E (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: β-type Ca2+ showed no correlation with the largest rupture force prior to calcium onset.
source: However, only low levels of β-type Ca2+ were resulted (Figure 6A,B), showing no correlation with the largest rupture force prior to calcium onset (Figure 6C,D, right ordinate), regardless of whether platelets were tested by A1WT (Figure 6A,C) or A1R1450E (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Much higher levels of Ca2+ of α- and β-types were induced by clamped forces applied to GPIbα via either A1WT or A1R1450E.
source: In sharp contrast, much higher levels of Ca2+ of α- and β-types were induced by clamped forces applied to GPIbα via either A1WT (Figure 6E,G) or A1R1450E (Figure 6F,H) despite their much lower levels than the rupture forces seen in the force-ramp experiments (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-H.

claim: The pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetime exhibited catch-slip bond behavior for A1WT and slip-only bond behavior for A1R1450E.
source: Concurrently, the longest of A1–GPIbα bond lifetimes that occurred prior to Ca2+ onset was measured on each platelet and averaged over all platelets in each group. This pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetime, tmax, exhibited catch-slip bond behavior for A1WT and slip-only bond behavior for A1R1450E (Figure 6G,H, right ordinate), just as the corresponding average bond lifetimes previously measured regardless of the intraplatelet calcium (Ju et al., 2013; Yago et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G,H and citations to prior work.

claim: The force-dependent pattern of calcium signals matched that of the pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetimes for both A1WT and A1R1450E.
source: Remarkably, the force-dependent pattern of calcium signals matched that of the pre-Ca2+ longest bond lifetimes for both A1WT and A1R1450E.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the data in Figure 6G,H.

claim: The ligand-independent positive correlation of Ca2+ signal with tmax is consistent with a previously observed inverse correlation between the cytosolic Ca2+ level and the translocation velocity of platelets on immobilized VWF.
source: The ligand-independent positive correlation of Ca2+ signal with tmax is consistent with a previously observed inverse correlation between the cytosolic Ca2+ level and the translocation velocity of platelets on immobilized VWF (Nesbitt et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and logical inference.

claim: The platelet translocation velocity is an inverse metric of VWF–GPIbα bond lifetime.
source: This is expected because the platelet translocation velocity is an inverse metric of VWF–GPIbα bond lifetime (Ju et al., 2013; Yago et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Platelets whose tests contained no unfolding event showed short tmax and low calcium of β- and null-types.
source: Platelets whose tests contained no unfolding event showed short tmax and low calcium of β- and null-types (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Platelets whose tests contained at least one pre-Ca2+ MSD unfolding event but no LRRD unfolding showed slightly longer tmax and higher Ca2+ of mostly α-type.
source: Platelets whose tests contained at least one pre-Ca2+ MSD unfolding event but no LRRD unfolding showed slightly longer tmax and higher Ca2+ of mostly α-type.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Only β-type Ca2+ was observed in the rare (2.6%) cases where LRRD unfolded but MSD did not.
source: By comparison, only β-type Ca2+ was observed in the rare (2.6%) cases where LRRD unfolded but MSD did not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The tmax values were much longer in cases where LRRD unfolded but MSD did not.
source: Since in these cases the tmax values were much longer, this data excludes tmax to be the direct determining parameter for the Ca2+ type.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: tmax is not the direct determining parameter for the Ca2+ type.
source: Since in these cases the tmax values were much longer, this data excludes tmax to be the direct determining parameter for the Ca2+ type.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that long tmax with LRRD unfolding but no MSD unfolding only produces β-type Ca2+.

claim: The group with pre-Ca2+ unfolding of both LRRD and MSD exhibited long tmax and high Ca2+ of mostly α-type.
source: Remarkably, the group with pre-Ca2+ unfolding of both LRRD and MSD exhibited long tmax and high Ca2+ of mostly α-type.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Platelets with a MSD unfolding event showed significantly longer tmax and higher calcium than those without when pulled by WM23.
source: Consistent results were obtained using WM23 to pull GPIbα to bypass LRRD unfolding (cf. Figure 2A), showing significantly longer tmax and higher calcium for platelets with than without a MSD unfolding event and a clear α- vs. β-type signal distinction between them (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: WM23 has higher α-type Ca2+ triggering efficiency than A1.
source: The higher α-type Ca2+ triggering efficiency of WM23 than A1 (compare MSD+ columns in Figure 7A and B) may be explained, at least in part, by the slower kinetics of GPIbα dissociation from WM23 than A1, which generated 70% more bond lifetime events by contacting a platelet for 200 s with WM23 than A1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WM23 generated 70% more bond lifetime events by contacting a platelet for 200 s than A1.
source: The higher α-type Ca2+ triggering efficiency of WM23 than A1 (compare MSD+ columns in Figure 7A and B) may be explained, at least in part, by the slower kinetics of GPIbα dissociation from WM23 than A1, which generated 70% more bond lifetime events by contacting a platelet for 200 s with WM23 than A1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WM23 bonds were 74% more durable than A1 bonds.
source: The bonds were also 74% more durable (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), resulting in a slightly higher (although not significant) MSD clamped unfolding probability per lifetime event for WM23 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The expected number of MSD clamped unfolding over a 200-s experimental period was significantly higher for WM23 than A1.
source: The expected number of MSD clamped unfolding over a 200-s experimental period, calculated as the product of the number of lifetime events and the unfolding probability per lifetime event, was significantly higher for WM23 than A1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The probability of platelet to have at least one MSD unfolding is 40% and 60% for A1 and WM23, respectively.
source: The probability of platelet to have at least one MSD unfolding, calculated as 1– (1– unfolding probability per lifetime event) ^ (# lifetime events), is 40% and 60% for A1 and WM23, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), close to the experimental results (51% vs. 69%, Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data and compared with observed results.

claim: Ramped forces generated very few MSD unfolding events and triggered only null/β- but not α-type Ca2+ regardless of whether A1WT or WM23 was used to pull.
source: Interestingly, despite their high levels, ramped forces generated very few MSD unfolding events and triggered only null/β- but not α-type Ca2+ regardless of whether A1WT or WM23 was used to pull (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Both force-induced MSD unfolding and bond lifetime are necessary for inducing α-type Ca2+ signal.
source: Together, these data indicate that both force-induced MSD unfolding and bond lifetime are necessary for inducing α-type Ca2+ signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ramped forces produce high rupture forces but short lifetimes and do not induce α-type Ca2+.

claim: tmax>2 s is the best predictor for A1WT to trigger α- rather than β-type Ca2+.
source: Using a sensitivity-specificity analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B) that slides a putative threshold through the tmax vs. Ca2+ type data, we found tmax>2 s to be the best predictor for A1WT to trigger α- rather than β-type Ca2+ (Figure 5E, dashed lines), which agrees with the fact that the 2 s threshold is much shorter than the average tmax of α-type Ca2+, but exceeds that of β-type Ca2+ and MSD time-to-unfold (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity-specificity analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: A longer-lived pre-Ca2+ bond favors MSD unfolding, thereby triggering α-type Ca2+; otherwise, it only triggers β-type Ca2+.
source: Thus, a longer-lived pre-Ca2+ bond favors MSD unfolding, thereby triggering α-type Ca2+; otherwise, it only triggers β-type Ca2+.
evidence: This is inferred from the threshold analysis and the relationship between bond lifetime and MSD unfolding.

claim: LRRD unfolding intensifies the Ca2+ level.
source: Together, our data suggests separate roles of LRRD and MSD unfolding in GPIbα signaling, with the former intensifying the Ca2+ level and the latter determining the Ca2+ signal type .
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing that LRRD unfolding increases Ca2+ intensity.

claim: MSD unfolding determines the Ca2+ signal type.
source: Together, our data suggests separate roles of LRRD and MSD unfolding in GPIbα signaling, with the former intensifying the Ca2+ level and the latter determining the Ca2+ signal type .
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing that MSD unfolding is required for α-type Ca2+.

claim: 14-3-3ζ is a cytoplasmic protein that has direct association with both GPIbα and GPIbβ C-termini.
source: 14-3-3ζ is a cytoplasmic protein that has direct association with both GPIbα and GPIbβ C-termini (Calverley et al., 1998) and regulates GPIb signal transduction(Dai et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 14-3-3ζ regulates GPIb signal transduction.
source: 14-3-3ζ is a cytoplasmic protein that has direct association with both GPIbα and GPIbβ C-termini (Calverley et al., 1998) and regulates GPIb signal transduction(Dai et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MPαC reduced the fraction of α-type Ca2+ from 34 to 3% without affecting β-type Ca2+.
source: Consistent with the previously reported signaling inhibition effect (Dai et al., 2005; Yin et al., 2013), MPαC reduced the fraction of α-type Ca2+ from 34 to 3% without affecting β-type Ca2+, whereas a scramble peptide MαCsc had no effect (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: A scramble peptide MαCsc had no effect on Ca2+ signaling.
source: Consistent with the previously reported signaling inhibition effect (Dai et al., 2005; Yin et al., 2013), MPαC reduced the fraction of α-type Ca2+ from 34 to 3% without affecting β-type Ca2+, whereas a scramble peptide MαCsc had no effect (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: GPIb–14-3-3ζ association is crucial for the transduction of MSD unfolding into intracellular signals.
source: Thus, GPIb–14-3-3ζ association, a biochemical event, is crucial for the transduction of MSD unfolding, a mechanical event, into intracellular signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking GPIb–14-3-3ζ association inhibits α-type Ca2+ signaling.

claim: GPIb–14-3-3ζ serves, at least in part, as a mechanotransducer.
source: These observations indicate that GPIb–14-3-3ζ serves, at least in part, as a mechanotransducer (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is inferred from the role of GPIb–14-3-3ζ in transducing MSD unfolding into Ca2+ signals.

claim: Pulling a single GPIbα by a 25 pN force for >2 s to unfold MSD once is necessary and sufficient to induce α-type Ca2+ signals.
source: Specifically, in 83% of the cases where α-type Ca2+ was triggered, only a single MSD unfolding event was observed before the Ca2+ onset. Of these, 43% had only one pre-Ca2+ bond lifetime event. Thus, pulling a single GPIbα by a 25 pN force for >2 s to unfold MSD once is necessary and sufficient to induce α-type Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In 83% of the cases where α-type Ca2+ was triggered, only a single MSD unfolding event was observed before the Ca2+ onset.
source: Specifically, in 83% of the cases where α-type Ca2+ was triggered, only a single MSD unfolding event was observed before the Ca2+ onset.
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data.

claim: Of the cases where α-type Ca2+ was triggered with a single MSD unfolding, 43% had only one pre-Ca2+ bond lifetime event.
source: Of these, 43% had only one pre-Ca2+ bond lifetime event.
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data.

claim: A threshold of force duration is required to trigger appreciable levels of α-type Ca2+.
source: In both cases a threshold of force duration is required, as ramped forces without a clamp phase are unable to trigger appreciable levels of α-type Ca2+ regardless of its magnitude.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ramped forces do not trigger α-type Ca2+ despite high magnitudes.

claim: Ramped forces without a clamp phase are unable to trigger appreciable levels of α-type Ca2+ regardless of its magnitude.
source: In both cases a threshold of force duration is required, as ramped forces without a clamp phase are unable to trigger appreciable levels of α-type Ca2+ regardless of its magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6A-D.

claim: A type 2B mutation, A1V1316M, causes additional signaling defects.
source: A recent study has shown a type 2B mutation, A1V1316M, causes additional signaling defects (Casari et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Another type 2B mutation, A1R1450E, also has signaling defect.
source: We showed that another type 2B mutation, A1R1450E, also has signaling defect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced Ca2+ signaling with A1R1450E.

claim: The defect to induce calcium has the same root as the binding defect, namely, the conversion of the wild-type catch-slip bond to the mutant slip-only bond.
source: Interestingly, the defect to induce calcium has the same root as the binding defect, namely, the conversion of the wild-type catch-slip bond to the mutant slip-only bond (Ju et al., 2013; Yago et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both binding and signaling defects are related to bond lifetime differences.

claim: Force exerted on GPIbα by A1R1450E is less able to unfold LRRD.
source: Consequently, force exerted on GPIbα by A1R1450E is less able to unfold LRRD, lasts shorter at 25 pN to unfold MSD less frequently, does not generate unbinding cooperativity between the LRRD and MSD, and induces lower level and frequency of α-type Ca2+ at >10 pN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A.

claim: Force exerted on GPIbα by A1R1450E lasts shorter at 25 pN to unfold MSD less frequently.
source: Consequently, force exerted on GPIbα by A1R1450E is less able to unfold LRRD, lasts shorter at 25 pN to unfold MSD less frequently, does not generate unbinding cooperativity between the LRRD and MSD, and induces lower level and frequency of α-type Ca2+ at >10 pN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: A1R1450E does not generate unfolding cooperativity between the LRRD and MSD.
source: Consequently, force exerted on GPIbα by A1R1450E is less able to unfold LRRD, lasts shorter at 25 pN to unfold MSD less frequently, does not generate unbinding cooperativity between the LRRD and MSD, and induces lower level and frequency of α-type Ca2+ at >10 pN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F,H.

claim: A1R1450E induces lower level and frequency of α-type Ca2+ at >10 pN.
source: Consequently, force exerted on GPIbα by A1R1450E is less able to unfold LRRD, lasts shorter at 25 pN to unfold MSD less frequently, does not generate unbinding cooperativity between the LRRD and MSD, and induces lower level and frequency of α-type Ca2+ at >10 pN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6F,H.

claim: The GPIbα mechanoreceptor can discriminate ligands.
source: These findings show that the GPIbα mechanoreceptor can discriminate ligands and shed light to the biophysical mechanisms of type 2B VWD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GPIbα responds differently to A1WT and A1R1450E.

claim: MSD unfolding is required to trigger α-type Ca2+.
source: In the present work, we found that MSD unfolding is required to trigger α-type Ca2+, showing that this extracellular mechanical event is necessary for transduction of the information embedded in the force waveform into intracellular biochemical signals via the 14-3-3ζ connection (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: MSD unfolding is necessary for transduction of the information embedded in the force waveform into intracellular biochemical signals via the 14-3-3ζ connection.
source: In the present work, we found that MSD unfolding is required to trigger α-type Ca2+, showing that this extracellular mechanical event is necessary for transduction of the information embedded in the force waveform into intracellular biochemical signals via the 14-3-3ζ connection (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of MSD unfolding requirement and 14-3-3ζ involvement in Ca2+ signaling.

claim: LRRD can feel the structural variation in the A1 and respond with an altered unfolding frequency and changed bond lifetime.
source: By overlapping with the ligand-binding site, the LRRD can feel the structural variation in the A1 and respond with an altered unfolding frequency and changed bond lifetime.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LRRD unfolding frequency differs between A1WT and A1R1450E.

claim: LRRD unfolding prolongs A1–GPIbα bond lifetime to facilitate MSD unfolding, thereby increasing the frequency of α-type Ca2+ and its level.
source: Importantly, LRRD unfolding prolongs A1–GPIbα bond lifetime to facilitate MSD unfolding, thereby increasing the frequency of α-type Ca2+ and its level (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between LRRD unfolding, bond lifetime, MSD unfolding, and Ca2+ signaling.

claim: The mechanosensor includes a MSD in the juxtamembrane region whose conformational change results in a binary decision of Ca2+ type.
source: Thus, our study has elucidated part of a mechanosensor that includes three components: 1) a MSD in the juxtamembrane region whose conformational change results in a binary decision of Ca2+ type,
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MSD unfolding determines whether α-type or β-type Ca2+ is triggered.

claim: The mechanosensor includes a LRRD in the ligand-binding region whose conformational change leads to continuous alterations in ligand-binding duration, signal level and fractions of different signal types.
source: 2) a LRRD in the ligand-binding region whose conformational change leads to continuous alterations in ligand-binding duration, signal level and fractions of different signal types,
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LRRD unfolding affects bond lifetime and Ca2+ intensity.

claim: The mechanosensor includes a MP stalk that transmits force over a distance and provides coupling between the two unfoldable domains.
source: and 3) a MP stalk that transmits force over a distance and provides coupling between the two unfoldable domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of cooperative unfolding between spatially separated domains.

claim: The differential unfolding behaviors of the LRRD and MSD in response to distinct force waveforms provide a simple mechanical mechanism for unfolding cooperativity.
source: The differential unfolding behaviors of the LRRD and MSD in response to distinct force waveforms provide a simple mechanical mechanism for unfolding cooperativity, by setting the response order such that LRRD unfolds first during force ramp to give more time for MSD to unfold during force clamp.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LRRD requires ramped force and MSD can unfold during clamped force.

claim: LRRD unfolds first during force ramp to give more time for MSD to unfold during force clamp.
source: The differential unfolding behaviors of the LRRD and MSD in response to distinct force waveforms provide a simple mechanical mechanism for unfolding cooperativity, by setting the response order such that LRRD unfolds first during force ramp to give more time for MSD to unfold during force clamp.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential unfolding pattern observed in the experiments.

claim: LRRD is a common structure shared by many adhesion and signaling receptors, e.g., toll-like receptors.
source: In addition, our findings may have broad implications since LRRD is a common structure shared by many adhesion and signaling receptors, e.g., toll-like receptors (Bella et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.
